utterances.text: And my last question to you is: Can you read us what's written on that stamp, the official stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The Serbian municipality of Ilijas, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," and this is the president of the municipality of Ilijas's stamp. When I needed to intervene on behalf of anybody, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- signed such a document and stamped it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I stop you there. Just read what's inside the document and not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is sitting too close to microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbian Republic of Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can that be enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a stamp that was valid between 4th of April and the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a stamp of the Serbian Ilijas Brigade. It says the Serbian Ilijas Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. Serbian Ilijas Brigade. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I have just realised that it is actually the stamp of the Ilijas Brigade, now that the document has been enlarged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which you signed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, if you allow me. Which was valid from the 4th of April until the 20th of May. That was the period during which the stamp was actually valid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And when you did sign, you signed it as the official in the Ilijas Brigade, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not during that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] People were leaving because of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could tender --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness -- no. Put on your earphones again. Witness, during the break, you should carefully consider whether you want to continue to answer questions that are not put to you, to give explanations which you're not asked to do, and not to follow instructions. If that is what you want to do, your position as a Defence witness might have to be reconsidered by this Chamber. So therefore suppress your apparent natural inclination to tell us what you want to tell us and focus on what we want you to tell us; that is, an answer to the questions that are put to you. Our patience is not without limitations. Let that be clear to you. Take your time to consider it. And it's time for a break now. We'll resume at five minutes past 12.00. But --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [In English] Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic wants to consult which he can do during the break, Mr. Lukic. You may follow the usher. We resume at five minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, do you have any plans with the last document on our screen, that is, the permission document?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, I tender 31131, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31131 receives number P6697, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Ms. Bibles, you earlier showed to the witness and you didn't tender three documents not signed by him but bearing his name. The Chamber wonders where they come from.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: They were seized by OTP from Sarajevo aid, Your Honour. Not as -- I'm just looking for a date. But they were all seized, like I said, from Aid Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And were they part of a larger series with sequential numbering --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of documents or? Or were they just more or less isolated?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Obviously these documents had this -- the code. If I could get back to the Court, I'd like to ask for a little more information, actually, about --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: -- the date of the seizure as well as the sequential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because the suggestion was that numbers were just invented for it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, there may be ways of, to some extent, verifying whether they fit into a series and whether they are then duplicates --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- same numbers but different documents. That's something to be carefully considered, perhaps, in this respect. Mr. Adzic, I hope you have had sufficient time to carefully consider my instructions and advice, and Ms. Bibles will now continue her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, I'd next like to show you 65 ter 3722. Sir, this appears to be a list for exchange of captured persons. And when it comes -- the document comes up, I would ask you --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We would go to last page, actually, first, and look at the signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no signature of mine on this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And perhaps if we could start at the front page.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This can't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In B/C/S, it can't be the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No, this isn't the first. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, sir, the top left-hand corner, although it's a little hard to see in the B/C/S version, this document reads Serbian municipality of Ilijas, number 100-03, date 25 June 1992. It's titled: "List for as Exchange of Captured Persons from Ilijas municipality for Persons Captured in Breza and Visoko Municipalities." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, this document, as we saw at the end, appears to have your name at the end although not a signature. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: I have never seen this document before. I recognise some of the names and I do know what situation it refers to, but this document has never been shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with these names as individuals who were captured in Ilijas municipality?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: Some of the last names do ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, this appears to be a five-page document, and apparently the B/C/S document is out of order.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll -- we'll fix that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second page is the original of the front page.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, this -- at the top of the right-hand top of the page is a reference to transcript, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you first seek an answer to your previous question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with those last names as individuals who were captured in Ilijas municipality, sir?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: I know some of the last names as people who lived in some of the villages in Ilijas municipality. I recognise some of them because I was not in a position to know them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, now I asked you to focus on the question. Now there was a question put to you, whether you recognise these names or perhaps some of them, as people that were captured. Did you know of any persons being captured in Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not know them personally. Not directly. But I do recognise some of the last names. They belonged to some people who lived in Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll stop you again. Were you aware of any persons being captured in Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not arrested individually or collectively. They were captured following combat operations as civilians. Upon their insistence, they were exchanged or so they wished to be, for people who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain to me how civilians then can be captured in combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In case of an attack by a unit from a Muslim village or a Muslim-held territory when there is combat, and if those Muslim units are defeated, whatever civilians are left behind are treated as captured persons by the army. They were captured in a combat zone, but the treatment they were accorded was as civilians. However, since they were in a combat zone, if there was still combat ongoing, they needed to be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me. So you captured civilians in combat zones. That's what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It happened as a consequence of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, so it happened. Did you release them after they were -- after combat was over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Free to go back to their own place where they lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had the right to choose. However, for the most part, they never asked to return. They asked to be allowed to leave for Muslim territory; that is to say, to territory under Muslim authority. We met their request and it was done that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they exchanged or were they just released in accordance with their wish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pursuant to their wish, they were allowed to leave for Muslim-controlled territory. By the same token, in agreement with the Muslim authorities of Breza and Visoko, the same was done for the Serb population who wished to move to Serb controlled territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, was it your responsibility to provide for those captured prisoners?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: It was done by bodies of the Red Cross. Of course, it was also my duty to assist the Red Cross, since I headed the municipal bodies, in order to provide whatever assistance was needed to secure those civilians and taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: When you refer to Red Cross in this time-period, June of 1992, are you referring to the Serbian Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. The president of the Serbian Red Cross was Veljko Mitar, who had been with the Red Cross for a number of years previously and was very dedicated to performing his job.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, where were these captured people held in Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: We did not have any facilities. If any facilities were used, they were mainly schools or halls with large premises so that food could be provided for them. They were held as long as necessary, usually for several days before the paperwork went through.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Was the paper work co-ordinated for these exchanges through the Republika Srpska Exchange Commission?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: At that moment in time, no. It was co-ordinated locally with the commission on the Muslim side as well as the Commission for Exchange of Ilijas Municipality, which was actually part of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd tender 65 ter 3722.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 3722 receives number P6697, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6697 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we please go to the page we saw earlier with a stamp and a signature. That could be page 1 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Madam, I have a question for the witness in relation to this page in B/C/S. It's a list of names beginning with number 91 and -- oh, no, there are many different numberings. I see a stamp and a signature there on the right-hand side. Mr. Adzic, can you explain whose signature we see here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't consider it to be my signature. The document is completely unknown to me. It looks very odd, and to me it's more of a counterfeit than a proper document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your name is written there. Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, well, you can see my name there. I can't explain how it came to be there. But the document is very strange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In addition to your name we see, at least in the English translation, "Crisis Staff President." That was your position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was. But the document itself, the original, well, you can see for yourself what it looks like. There is nothing I can say about it. I assert that I have never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, you gave us the last exhibit number as P6697. What was the number of 4 -- 65 ter 31131.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. It should be number P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So document 3722 receives number P6698 not 97. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now being corrected. 6698 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to shift topics and direct attention towards paragraph 28 of your statement. In that paragraph you indicate that Mladic visited "our front two or three times during the war." Can you give us the dates and locations where General Mladic visited during the war?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact dates, and I'd rather not speculate because it was a long time ago. The location was the brigade command. General Mladic invited me to tour some other parts, such as the health centre. He wanted to know the situation with the supplies and how the people were going about their every day lives, whether they had sufficient reserves. He simply wanted to have that kind of information and I provided it to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you have any idea where in the war -- was this early in the war, the middle of the war, the end of the war, in terms of dates?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: I think the first time was around October 1993. After that, it was in 1994 once or twice. But it was already 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And I'd next like to shift directions to your tenure as minister of interior in 1993. Do you agree the previous minister of the interior was Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And you were appointed, I believe it's in your statement, in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: On the 20th of January.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like to ask just a couple of questions or go into a few areas of some of your actions as the Republika Srpska minister of police. I'd like to start by asking about Simo Drljaca. Wasn't he the chief of police in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could have P3951, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, this is a 1 KK morale report. It's a 1st Krajina Corps report on the state of combat morale dated 3 September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And I'd ask that we go to page 4 in the English and in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, sir, while in the English we'll be looking at the top of the page, you'll be looking at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S. Here in the document it states that Prijedor police -- it states that the Prijedor police under Simo Drljaca "committed a massacre in the Skender Vakuf area of over 150 men who wanted to leave the ARK." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: I'm trying to -- yes, I see it. Towards the bottom. Let me read it first. Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, the Chamber has received evidence that this massacre was known to members of the Bosnian Serb leadership and to the Main Staff of the VRS in August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I could refer to Exhibits D58 and P4239.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As minister of the interior, you knew about this massacre, didn't you? Though it preceded your time in the ministry, you were aware of this as minister?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of it at all, and no one provided me with any kind of information in the ministry regarding it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to now go to 65 ter 31103. And, sir, this appointed Simo Drljaca as a member of the commission for investigating genocide. And, sir, we see this is type-signed by you on May 15th 1993 appointing Mr. Drljaca as a member of the commission for investigating crimes of genocide against the Serbian people. Now, it describes him as head of the information office in the cabinet of the minister of the interior. That's you, correct?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca was appointed advisor on proposal from the CSB in Banja Luka. He was not proposed to act as commission president. I am not aware of it and I also see that the signature on the document is illegible.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree as minister of the interior this is an area under your control, isn't it? Or your authority.

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: In the sense of the functioning of the ministry, yes. But at that time I had only arrived and started acquainting myself with the situation. At that moment, I had no information related to any events wherever in our territory save for the territory of Ilijas municipality. I only had information about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, when you were appointed minister of the interior, you're saying your only base of information was your personal observations from Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: Anything that happened before the 20th of January is limited to the information I received in Ilijas. I was there all the time. There was no possibility for me to communicate, and it was not within my competence to be interested in any other part of Republika Srpska. When I assumed my position as minister of the interior, I only began acquainting myself with the situation in the rest of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Weren't you also a member of the SDS Main Board starting in 1991 which had much broader authority than Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: The Main Board was a political body. By a decision of the SDS president, Mr. Karadzic, in April the work of the SDS in political terms was frozen. In the political sense, it continued working only in 1993. It was because of the war. So that there would be no political rifts and arguments. The Main Board did not even meet, let alone discuss any issues during that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Adzic, we are talking about 1993. The document on the screen before you is dated 15 May 1993. At that point in time, you were almost four months minister of the interior. It was not just the situation when you acquainted yourself with the situation. It was four months later. Could you consider your answer if that was correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer stands. My position in the ministry and the situation that prevailed in the ministry was such that simply didn't know what I can do, and I could not receive information that was not forwarded to me through lower levels where some of the decisions were made. I was simply unable to receive such information. It rested with the CSBs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Adzic, Ms. Bibles asked you - and that was the beginning of the line of questioning - if Mr. Simo Drljaca was head of the information office in your cabinet as minister of the MUP. Can you please now answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was appointed, and I believe that the decision was issued in the course of May, but he actually never assumed the position. He stayed in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But what position are you talking, member of the commission for investigating crimes of genocide or head of the information office in the cabinet of the minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His official position was in the information service. As for all the other activities of his, I'm not familiar with any of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Adzic, that exactly was the question of Ms. Bibles at the beginning of this line of questioning. It could have been very easy to answer that question just to say "yes."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I tender 31103.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31103 receives number P6699, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Ms. Bibles, I have, in relation to this, you showed the witness documents, but the first names of Mr. Drljaca are not the same in the one we see now, the Simo, and in the previous one, which was a different first name. Stevo. Not Simo. Could you please have a look at it and perhaps later explain why you nevertheless, as you suggested, them to be the same persons, that's one. Second, in the document, the list which was not in the right order, we see that there are duplicates in the numbers. There is one part which apparently has been torn apart and perhaps put together again. But that seems at least not to be the same list. Therefore, the Chamber would seriously be informed about what makes you present to a witness something that looks as one list but where under the same numbers we find different names and to further clarify that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Absolutely. I'll be right -- I'll chase that information down and report it back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'd like to. And if that has -- well, the witness said he hadn't seen that list anyhow, so therefore he may not have been confused by it. But let's keep in mind that if you present something in this way that witnesses may be confused by it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, your tenure as minister of the RS MUP was somewhere between six and nine months. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: From the 20th of January up until the 12th of July 1993. Yes, six months, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Isn't it true that your resignation was not accepted until September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: It is true. My resignation was accepted at the session presided by President Karadzic. However, the Assembly of Republika Srpska subsequently held its session and ratified that decision and appointed a deputy minister. I myself resigned on the 12th of June. I'm not sure about the date, but it was in early July and as of that date I stopped holding that office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that when you said the 12th of June, that you misspoke and that you wanted to refer to the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] July. July. It was in July.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be helpful to look at 65 ter 18899.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, this is the official decision about the dismissal -- your dismissal from the post. All right. Sir, does this refresh your recollection, that your resignation was accepted by President Karadzic on the 17th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: On the 17th of September, he appointed Tomo Kovac as the acting minister. I submitted my written resignation at the beginning of July, and then at a session attended by President Karadzic and other members of the presidency my resignation was accepted. And now we are talking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the simple question was: Was your resignation accepted by President Karadzic on the 17th of September? The answer, apparently, is yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President Karadzic accepted my resignation on the 12th of July at that session. And this is just a written decision stating the fact that as of the 12th of July, I had no longer acted as the minister of police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, Witness, this decision doesn't state that you are dismissed as of the 12th of July. Where do you see it on this document that your resignation was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see it either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, I am referring to --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender 65 ter 18899.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 18899 receives number P6700, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Witness, in all fairness, I have to tell you that when we asked whether he accepted your resignation, when no specific reference to at that time in that question to the document was made, that what you wanted to tell us apparently was that he orally ordered -- a decision was made on the 12th of July which was then put on paper and signed on the 17th of September. That short explanation would have fitted well into the question that was put to you, although you confused us a bit by the way in which you started your answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put an additional question. Who carried out the function of the Ministry of the Police between the 12th of July and the 17th of September 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tomislav Kovac, who was the chief of public security when I was minister, and that was decided on the 17th of July. And that decision was made by President Karadzic himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was decided on the 17th of July, five days after your resignation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see that decision issued on the 17th of July. It is possible. After my written resignation that I handed in at that meeting, I no longer received any information about the work of the Ministry of the Interior, nor did I receive any document from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, shifting to -- back to your statement. In paragraph 14, you described that rumours and estimates put Serb casualties at 6.000 in Sarajevo during the war. In this estimate, did you mean to include both civilians and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, according to the information we heard and that the witnesses conveyed to us, the first casualties were members of the Serbian Democratic Party who were besieged in Sarajevo. In Sarajevo itself, there were no Serbian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement you proffer a number of casualties in Sarajevo. The next question would be, when you say Sarajevo, do you mean the city centre, the urban municipalities that make up the core of Sarajevo, or some other area?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: I mean the part of Sarajevo which was under the control of Muslim authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, do you know what the sources, specific sources of information are for these estimates?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: They were refugees from Sarajevo and one of the sources are the Sarajevo media. In 1996, they wrote about those figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So you don't -- you don't know whether these numbers, then, maybe have come from the Sarajevo household survey in 1994 or the Bosnian Book of the Dead or other sources that list casualties?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: I read that in the Bosnian media such as Slobodna Bosna and Avaz. To put it simply, people talked.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you know whether this estimate includes Serbs who died violently and Serbs who died of natural causes or both?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: I suppose that this refers to the Serbs who died of violent causes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, the OTP has employed demographers over the years to analyse various sources to determine as accurate of information as possible in an objective manner. For instance, an expert demographer employed statistical analysis and concluded that a minimum number of several hundred Serbs had indeed been violently killed in Sarajevo between April 1992 and November of 1995. Would you agree that this would be a more reliable source for these casualties than your estimates that you put in your report?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Based on?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Those analyses should be shown to the witness. How can we analyse or comment something on which he has never seen or read or analysed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the witness has not given any of the estimates of any of the sources, he's said to that. But if you -- the simple question is whether the witness would, and then perhaps we could rephrase that in general terms, whether a careful demographic statistical analysis, whether that would not be a better basis for estimates of numbers of people who have died. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One more thing, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have we seen, has the Defence at all seen these estimates?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour, they have been disclosed and in fact, if you look at 65 ter 11854 -- actually, 65 ter 11854 through 11859 would be the Sarajevo demographic reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, a totally different matter. Whether the witness would consider rumours and estimates he has seen in newspapers in 1996 a better source than a thorough statistical demographic analysis may not be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Done by the Prosecution. It is not experts who are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you know that? You said you didn't even know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. But Ms. Bibles said their --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Their employed so-called experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you say that if you're employed, for example, by the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Claiming that only a couple of hundred Serbs were killed in Sarajevo is an insult and not only not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's Muslim propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether it's propaganda or not. We will -- you take it very seriously. We are talking about -- are you talking about civilians or -- and Sarajevo, within, and that's what the witness said, we are talking about Serbs who had died from violent causes in the territory which was controlled by the BiH, and the witness said it was civilians. Okay. If you say that this is an insult, then perhaps the parties should exchange views on that and see whether that's true and otherwise make submissions. Because, Mr. Lukic, if this is a clear distortion of reality in serious demographic reports, that would shed a light on the way in which the Prosecution approaches this case and should be taken very seriously. At the same time, whether the witness, who bases his number on rumours and what he read in the media, whether the witness considered this to be better than demographic reports, he doesn't know, seems not to be of vital importance for the Chamber to know. But, Ms. Bibles, I think there is a matter --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to be discussed and to be taken seriously.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Very much so, Your Honour. And I would point out my question. As the Court is aware, demographers work in minimums and maximums and look at statistical evaluations. And that is the point I was trying to make is the difference between what this witness proffered to the Trial Chamber. And I a hundred per cent agree with the Trial Chamber, that this is an area that the Defence and Prosecution need to sit down and have a -- have a serious conversation about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A serious conversation is needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Chamber would like to be informed about any continuing -- continuing dispute about this or whether the parties would come closer to each other. Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, sir, finally I want to address your perspective given in your statement that you seem to portray the blockade as being a Muslim-driven means of locking people out of the city. I'd like to have you look at Exhibit 31107. This is a media source in which you were quoted, and I'd like you to look at the quote, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In the English, we're looking at the second paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In B/C/S, that's -- I'm trying to find. It's the top, I believe, of that second column. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apparently not the whole of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, of the quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the article is translated. I see as a date the 14th of -- it seems, is that December 1993? Perhaps the witness could assist us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Top left-hand corner, just below the word "klas" [phoen] there is a date. Could you read that aloud for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tuesday, the 14th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, first have you had an opportunity to read your quote?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: Yes, I read it partly, and I can say that this was not a joint session of the municipality of Ilijas and Vogosca. This was a session of the assembly of Serbian Sarajevo, the city assembly of Serbian Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, let's try this a different way. I'm going to read the English translation of at least part of your quote and ask you if it accurately depicts what you said. "'I am convinced that the war will end when we take Sarajevo. Unless they are defeated militarily, there will be no life for us here,' emphasized President Adzic, adding that the Serbian people was aware that 'if they cordoned off Sarajevo the Serbs would get a state of their own.'" Sir, is that quote from you accurate?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that it was Serb forces who closed Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: It is not true. First, the Muslim forces closed Sarajevo from the inside, and then to defend the Serbian areas around Sarajevo we established our own defence line.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles. Are you tendering the document or it has been read into the -- we have the date, we have the literal quote, and the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have probably 10 to 15 minutes. Maybe 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps we could do that -- 10 minutes would fit into the next session, more or less. If you'd prefer to take the break first, then the Chamber would not oppose that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My math is very bad today, Mr. Lukic. Until the break, we have 15 minutes left, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can see P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take the break first because not my math is only bad but that of my colleagues is not accurate either. So the Chamber is in a bad mathematical state. I deplore that. Witness, we'll continue in 20 minutes from now. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No loud speaking, not even about mathematics. We take a break and will resume at 20 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, if there is any way in re-examination you could pay attention to or otherwise inform the Chamber about the assembly decision on which basis in December 1991 the Crisis Staff in Ilijas was established, which was not a secret matter but an open matter. I don't know whether you have any clue as to what decision the witness was referring to. One of my problems was that we hardly find anything of the kind in his statement. There is even more in your summary than there is in the statement, which is, by the way, not the way -- the 65 ter summary, that -- I think there is even more in it than in the statement itself which, of course, is not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When I read the statement, Your Honours, I also noticed that there is no -- nothing clear about the Crisis Staff. That's why I tried to clarify it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if the basis for the establishment of the Crisis Staff which, I think the witness said, was a decision taken by the assembly and it was in December 1991, then, of course, other things have happened in December 1991 as well which are also related, to some extent, to further developments. At least that's evidence the Chamber has received. Then I would like to clearly be able to make a distinction between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to clarify it with the witness or do you want us to provide the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you have the document. But perhaps you put it to the witness and say, "Is this the document you're referring to the about the decision?"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have it with me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. We have to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you lead this evidence, then I take it that you have some thoughts about what the witness was referring to rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I tried to find it. I was not able to find it when I was preparing the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's see then to what extent we can explore it with the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Adzic, you'll now be re-examined by Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But this will then take a bit more than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, depending on what answers we get.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day to you, Mr. Adzic, one more time. As you were entering, we were discussing something that you probably were not able to hear. The Chamber is interested in whether you could be more accurate in terms of what document was used to establish your Crisis Staff. As you said, it was in December 1991.

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: Based on a dispatch signed by the RS president, Mr. Karadzic. I apologise. It was based on a dispatch that I received as the president of the municipality from President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to have that dispatch in your possession?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: No. It remained in the archives of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you presume that we would be able to find it?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: Provided the archives are still in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you approximate in terms of date? Was it at the beginning or end of December?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: It may have been around the 20th or the 21st of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That ends that particular topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, perhaps if you would not mind, I would follow-up on the answers. There is evidence before this Chamber about a document dated the 19th of December, which was distributed to the various municipalities, at least the Serb leadership in those municipalities. A document which was not signed by Mr. Karadzic but a document which set out, as it's often referred to, Variant A and Variant B; that is, how to prepare in the near future your Serb institutions within municipalities. Variant A and B distinguishing between municipalities which were of a Serb majority, as far as population is concerned, and a Serb minority and then in two different stages. And earlier a first stage, and then a second stage. That is what this Chamber is aware of and is familiar with. Now, if I have described this document in the way I did, is that the type of document you are referring to or is it something really different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be document A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, in the same document Variant A and Variant B are described, the one to be adopted in - and forgive me if it was the Serb majority or minority municipalities - but the one Variant A applicable in a -- some of the municipalities, either majority or minority, I don't remember; and the other one to be applied in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are you referring to a document when you said, "We established a Crisis Staff upon the instruction of the assembly ...," signed by Mr. Karadzic? Are you referring to a document in which Variants A and B were described, where you said A would apply for Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recall exactly. I can only try to recall the instructions we received. Since the Serbs were in the majority in our municipality, I suppose that it would entail document A as you interpret it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I told you that I was talking about a document in which both the A variant and the B variant were described. One document, Variant A, to do this and this and this in two different stages; Variant B, to do this and this and this in two stages. Is that the type of document you are referring to? Because the -- there is no other document known to either the Defence at this moment nor to the Prosecution; whereas, the parties and the Bench are quite familiar with the document as I described it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it could be the document, and Variant A would be applicable to our situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, that document, how did you receive that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was by telegram, by telex via electronic communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the document I described and with which many in this courtroom are very familiar was not a public document. To the contrary, it was strictly confidential. Therefore, I'm asking you again whether the instructions you received really were public and adopted in an assembly session, I think you said the Assembly of the Republika Srpska, or whether it could have been a document which was confidential rather than public and not adopted in a -- in an assembly session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document arrived by telex. It was signed, although I cannot say with any certainty whether it was signed by President Karadzic or the speaker of the assembly. It contained instructions on how to establish the Crisis Staff. As for any further details or the template that was used, that is something I cannot recall. It could be that it was signed. I just remember that it arrived by telex. It was a kind of dispatch. And I followed the instructions received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I leave it to that and I invite the parties to search for whatever other document around the same date which would be of guidance in establishing Crisis Staffs publicly adopted in any assembly session. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] I have to stress the following: When I was told that it was a dispatch, I tried to find a short document containing several lines. I wasn't paying attention to any variants A or B. But I will continue with my questions. First, I would like to see P3797.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Adzic, once we have the document on the screen, you will see that it comes from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps dated the 27th of May, 1992. In item 2, which is in the last third of your page, you were asked about the establishment of the MAD. You said that at the time, it had not been established. I wanted to draw your attention to the following. We have a percentage stated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we have -- number 2 is only on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's on the English version in the next page. Sorry, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For example, the brigade armoured levels were only up to 30 per cent of what was necessary and only 20 per cent in terms of 60-millimetre mortars and so on and so forth. Were you familiar with that at all in terms of the number of assets the brigade had at the moment of establishment?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: I was familiar because I had been informed about it by the brigade command. I knew that the brigade was poorly equipped in that regard. Of course, I did have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we next have 3714, 65 ter. I don't know what is the P number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is document P6695, MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the document -- yes, we have it. Could I ask the witness. You say there was only a certain percentage of the mortars which you would need, and I'm still talking about the previous document, could you tell us how many 60-millimetre mortars the Ilijas Brigade had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say. I really don't know. That information was shared with me at a session, but only the command and the people who were in command had that information available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whether they were poorly equipped, yes or no, you have no numbers for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I did not go into analysing that. I only relied on the information presented to me by the command. They presented the facts and of course I trusted my command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They presented their conclusions and not the facts because you didn't know how many mortars of 60-millimetres they had, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was summary data based on individual units analyses. The units were not considered individually at such kind of meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I showed you the document on the screen to tell you what I'm going to be talking about. This is about you asking for three to five tanks. And then after that, we saw P353. I can't see what page was used. I have not made a note of that. Just a moment please, bear with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps Ms. Bibles could assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be page 155 in English and 154 in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can have the pages Judge Fluegge just mentioned, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here and this is a document which says that on Saturday the 13th of June - i.e., a day after the letter by which you addressed President Karadzic - it says that a meeting was held with the presidency. On the 13th of June, did you attend a meeting with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: No, not on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't know who presented this?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: I suppose that it was Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you don't know, do you? You just assume.

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now just briefly, P6697.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have discussed this document at great length already. Just for the record, it should be noted that the abbreviation SIBr at the top of the document was very often interpreted as the Sarajevo-Ilijas Brigade; however, we can see in the stamp that it was the 1st Serbian Ilijas Brigade. So I would like this to be corrected everywhere in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Let me just.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the stamp, you can see in the inner circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we can't change the transcript. If the words are spoken, then they should be transcribed as spoken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted it to be noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should be noted. Then you said in the stamp we could that -- could we enlarge the stamp in detail? The original. What we see is the Srpska Republika Bosnia Herzegovina, that's the outline. Then we have the "Srpska Obstina" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the middle circle is the "Srpska Obstina Ilijas." Yes. Now, Witness, could you read the most inner circle of this stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 1st Serbian Ilijas Brigade. That was a stamp of the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look now, Mr. Lukic. Yes. That is -- now could we ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you have a look at the original at the left top corner. Could we move to that. There you see the command of what exactly? Could you tell us what it stands for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The command of the 1st Serbian Ilijas Brigade in Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I -- Ms. Bibles, I'm looking at you as well. Would you agree that the reference is -- the abbreviation, although from the letters you could make anything out of the S you want to but that it's the most logical explanation that it would be the 1st Serb Ilijas Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I think that's obviously out of my area of expertise, but, yes, I agree with the conclusion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we have corrected that on the record. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Adzic, it was my impression that you wanted to add something to your explanation of this document. Can you remember now what it was? What was it that you wanted to add to your explanation?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: Are you talking --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When we were discussing this document, you wanted to say something but there was no question to prompt you to do that. Do you know what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: Can you tell us if you ever seen this document which is now on
utterances.text: I wanted to say that when the Ilijas Brigade was set up, the brigade was given its stamp. And I, as the president of the municipality, had my own stamp. So this is a document that was drafted in situations which were not within the purview of the brigade command. I can explain. There was a pressure of people and the Red Cross not to allow exit to some Muslims whose families remained in Visoko and elsewhere, and they made their exit conditional. I opposed that and I said that no conditions should be set. And since the command could not resolve those issues and at the check-points only the decisions of the command was valid, the command issued this document and then I used my authority to act and to help them go through. It would take a lot of time for me to explain how much pressure was present at the time. I didn't want to. I could not prevent people from going where they wanted to go, and only in exceptional cases I had to react in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now -- and let's look at another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you would not mind, I would have some follow-up questions in this respect as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who gave instructions to the check-points, who to let go through and where there were doubts as whether people should be stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The check-points were manned by army members sometimes working together with the police, and only people with valid passes were let through. That was a guarantee that that movement had been approved and that it was controlled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, who gave those instructions? You told us what happened, but who had instructed them to only allow people through with valid passes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Civilian passes were issued by the Red Cross and that was not in dispute. You saw that there were agreements between the Muslim side and the Red Cross. I said there was never a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. Who told the check-points only to allow civilians through with valid Red Cross documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a decision of the appropriate security organs, and it was intended for the control of everybody's movement. So nobody could move without a valid pass within a certain area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who were the appropriate security organs you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the separation line, it was the security organs of the brigade commander and the security organs of the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And as we have seen in many documents, you were presented as the command of the brigade, as even the commander of the brigade. So was it under your responsibility that these instructions were given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is an exceptional case. I already explained that to Mr. Lukic. It was beyond the scope of the brigade command. They couldn't do with civilian affairs. The situation was difficult and I used my authority to help those people who wanted to leave. My authority was of such a nature that the command could issue a document, I then cosigned or signed and confirmed the validity of that document with my stamp and signature, and then those people would no longer have any problems with leaving the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why didn't you send an order as commander of the 1st Serbian Ilijas Brigade to any check-points, that they should not stop elderly ladies or very young children of 7 years old at check-points? Why didn't you do that instead of upkeeping a system in which apparently you had instructed that people should be accompanied by Red Cross documents even if they are 59-year-old ladies or 7-year-old children? Why didn't you take such measures rather than to use your authority to lead these people through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could undertake measures only based on the situation as it was. The checkpoints were in the combat zones on the separation lines. Only in exceptional cases when pressure was put even on me to prohibit exit to some Muslims whose families had remained living in Visoko and Breza did they ask me to use my authority and request for them to be exchanged. And when some people, like, for example, these four citizens came to me, I used my authority. Pressure was put even on the Red Cross to forbid them to leave the territory, and in those exceptional situations, I used my authority to help such people. But those were original exceptional cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was exceptional in the circumstances here with this family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The exceptional circumstance was as follows: A lot of Serbs who had fled from Visoko and Breza knew that a lot of the families were blocked in those municipalities and they were not allowed to cross over to Ilijas. And then the members of those families put pressure on me and on the Red Cross, on the president of the Red Cross. At one point, the president of the Red Cross even wanted to resign as a result of these pressures. I asked him, telling him that he was the only capable person to deal with humanitarian issues, regardless of the pressures and the burden. I asked him to try and stick it out. And if situations were difficult, I told him to come and ask me for assistance. So in such situations, he indeed came to me and asked me to use my authority, which is what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I carefully listen to your answer, you're referring to families, Serb families, that were blocked in Visoko and Breza. Now, do I have to understand this that pressure was put upon you that Muslims could only leave if they - these families - would be allowed to come to Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Accordingly to the principle of reciprocity, Serbs were supposed to leave Breza and Visoko, and then we in our turn should let these people go. That was the pressure that was put on me. I couldn't do that. I didn't think that there should be any conditions and that's why I intervened. I thought that people should be allowed to move freely irrespective of the fact whether any of the Serbs would be allowed to leave the territories where they were staying at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which, in my view, then perhaps should have resulted in an order: Never stop elderly women and children, for the reasons you used until now, that is, that it should only be on the basis of reciprocity because there should no reciprocity. That's what one should expect under those circumstances. Do you have any comment on giving this permission rather than to issue instructions as I suggested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could issue such an instruction. However, neither the elderly women nor any of the civilians would ever come closer to the separation line without the previous guarantees issued by the organs that would send them there, because those should be previous negotiations about a cease-fire, the safety of crossing, and so on and so forth, and we could never do that without a co-operation with the Muslim side. No civilian ever did that spontaneously because they would have found themselves in a combat zone if they had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we please look at P6698. [In English] We should probably have another page in English version since it's not -- no, no, no. I need that page in B/C/S and then the corresponding page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, at the same time we asked the Prosecution to clarify some of the issues. I do not know whether you want to deal with those or with other matters. If you are dealing with other matters, then please proceed. If, however, you are addressing the same issues I raised with the Prosecution, then perhaps we could consider --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Or maybe without bothering the witness I can just ask how come that on this page there is a signature, alleged signature, of this gentleman, or at least his name, in the middle of the document when we can see the continuation of the names underneath?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It has got something to do with the -- the witness doesn't know the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He does not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- let's first listen to Ms. Bibles --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I accept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what explanations she has for this cut and glued together document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is a document from our rules of the road collection. It was an original document that had been torn up and pieced back together. I can say in terms of the translations to address your concerns. On the first B/C/S page, which is this one, it corresponds to the English page 3 in e-court. The second page in B/C/S corresponds to the English page 1 and 2. And then the third page in B/C/S corresponds to the English on page 5. So they're -- they're not matched in terms of the way that they come. But in terms of the history of the document, that's where -- where this one came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What surprises me -- and apparently the witness has no knowledge of the document. What surprises me that if this is torn in two pieces and then reconstructed, then at least the sequence of numbers comes as a surprise unless you would have created a document where after 129 you continue with most likely 29 or 31 and then after 144 you restart with 56 and then -- I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My colleague draws my attention to the fact at a left column on this page ends with 129, and then the next column starts with 130. But it's still -- it's a huge puzzle and what especially is of concern to me is that if you look at the numbers, then the numbers here and the numbers on the other pages give different names. Let's have a look at. That's what I tried to explain earlier as well. Oh, let me see.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, is that between the translations? Is that the concern? I think these are different lists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are two lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: -- of individuals. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are two lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness can't assist us, perhaps we should deal with the matter alert. Mr. Lukic, if you have any further questions, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't have any further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A very quick way of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Adzic, thank you again for having answered our questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the questions in re-examination triggered any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this concludes your evidence, Mr. Adzic. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you, even sometimes a bit more, the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise if I was too fast or too general in my answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have ten minutes left. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into closed session. Yes, we need the assistance -- can we have some amateurs to assist in pulling the curtains down.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We'll adjourn for the day and we will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 27th of August, in this same courtroom, I, at 9.30, and the first thing we'll do is to move into closed session tomorrow. And we stand adjourned.
